GTA Theft Auto: Vice City is another popular series of games about the world of crime, and the users of the community, a kind of extension of the part - Grand Theft Auto 3. The action takes place in the 1980s and is located in the new city of Vice City, to which Tom Vercetti (i.e. the player) is connected by Sonny Forelli to rule "order" with local gangs, Cuban gangsters and corrupt cops.

Why didn't I play GTA Vice city definitive edition? I didn't play it because I think the game has a lot of bugs and the graphics aren't that great, so I decided to finish the story in the original GTA Vice City. A huge minus for Rockstar Games that they removed the original parts from Steam.

✅80s atmosphere,
✅Beaches full of people on a sunny day (It gave a great effect and a feeling of realism)
✅Nice graphics, shining sun,
✅Interesting and funny plot,
✅Very atmospheric soundtrack (Radio stations with classics Michael Jackson, Africa e.t.c)
✅Optimization
✅Additional missions (firefighter, police, paramedic e.t.c mission)
✅Fast cars,
✅The ability to fly planes and helicopters (in GTA 3 it was impossible),
✅A lot of side missions (The downside is that these side missions are necessary to push the plot forward)
✅The ending is really surprising, it's just great
✅A lot of weapon selection (minigun bazooka)
✅Quite a large map
✅Open world

❌Too short dialogues
❌no swimming option
❌In my opinion few cars
❌Very poor helicopter control
❌Some missions are maddening and make you want to quit this game (2 missions with a plane, but also other missions on land)
❌incompatibility with the requirements of the launch systems (Windows 8, 8.1, 10), but what's surprising when the game is 16 years old,

Do the veteran GTA fans remember getting on the Faggio “Moped” at the beginning of the game, hearing Billie Jean on Flash FM and then the weather report came on saying bridges have been closed due to the storm? After all those years, this game still have a special place in my heart.

Search for the original GTA III, Vice City, and San Andreas ports or the 6 gen console versions on reseller sites or ebay, instead of touching Definitive.

Removing this game was inexcusable, no matter how marketers or Rockstar supporters will try to spin it.

You can't be seriously this short sighted. Now Grove Streets name is even further rung through the mud than it was back when they were War Drum. You did that Rockstar, just like how you forced this review.

Also go visit Silent's Blog if you end up getting the PC versions.

Before it gets said this review focuses on irrelevant content, Rockstar put out an update that changed this games availability. An option on the end users side was changed for the worst.

[b]Almost 20 years ago Vice City was one of the most varied, complete and alive digital cities ever created. An impressive playground for an impressive game, today, the game is still a great open-world with a strong character driven narrative and a deeply satirical and parodistic view of American society in the 80s[/b]

[h1]First Rundown[/h1]
Tommy Vercetti arrives in a town brimming with delights and degradation. He is fresh out of prison after serving a long stint for the mob and has been sent to Miam...Vice City by his former boss in order to start a new business. A crucial drug handover goes wrong and the money gets pinched, Tommy is straight in at the deep end with a debt to pay on top of making a respectable name for himself in his new home. 

[b]Grand Theft Auto: Vice City[/b] is a 2002 [b]open-world action-adventure game[/b]. It’s played in third-person and the open-world design lets the player freely roam Vice City by foot, car, motorbike, boat, helicopter and plane. The game's plot is based on multiple real-world events that happened in Miami in the 1980s such as the Cubans-Haitians war, the biker gangs invasion, the crack epidemic or the glam metal fever. The most strong and evident influence cames by movies and television of the era, including Scarface and Miami Vice. Does this patchwork of content work? Magnificently. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2336578236

[h1]
WHAT IT IS AND HOW IT WORKS
[/h1]
[h2][b]Story[/b][/h2]
◼️ [b]Writing[/b] 
It’s a long road to find out who stole the boss's money and pay them back, Tommy needs to make some new friends and a tidy buck on the side for his activities, for his new business. The writing gives you the feeling of a large, gradually unravelling plot. Quests are funny, dumb and nonsensical, taking part in the tale is a pleasure. To get the traitor you have to dirt your hands: drive taxis, get involved in a turf war between the Cubans and the Haitians, befriend a Scottish rock group named Love Fist, smash up the local mall for protection money, demolish a building to lower real estate prices (fucking quest with the helicopter toy), hook up with a biker gang, run an adult film studio, rob a bank, and much, much more.
◼️ [b]Characters and dialogues[/b] 
Mr Vercetti is a fully realised character with plenty to say for himself, he interacts with the major and not-so-major characters in town through a mostly amusing and well-acted script, stuffed with amusing accents and odd series in-joke. The game's large cast of characters is colourful and memorable, stereotypes of real people, made upon the likeness of the ones seen on television police shows.

[h2][b]Gameplay[/b][/h2]
◼️ [b]How it plays and nice features[/b] 
As a third-person open-world, [b]Vice City is arcade to the core[/b] and the missions involve a nice variety of gameplay. Worldbuilding plays a big role in the approach to an objective. Some buildings can be entered, some can be used as a landing pad for helicopters, some can be bought, opening up a new range of missions and rewards. Weapons and vehicles variety is huge as well, Tommy can’t still swim but he can ride a boat and fly. 
◼️ [b]Overall difficulty[/b] 
Overall Vice City gives a lot of challenge to the players. Mostly because of the “wanted stars” you get by doing some “mischief”. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2334866539
[h2][b]Visuals[/b][/h2]
◼️ [b]Art Design[/b] 
As a parody of 1980s Miami, Rockstar North has done a fantastic job of constructing a believable set of islands with appropriately garish neon-lined urban architecture, Cuban and Haitian populated ghettos and disgustingly rich areas dotted with mansions complete with golf courses and jetties, yachts and all.
Despite the age, the animation is still nice, with body language playing an important role in the portrayal of the story, cars are nicely constructed and the city architecture surrounding them is still cool to see.

[h2][b]Soundtrack and Audio[/b][/h2]
◼️ [b]Music, audio effects[/b] 
The radio entertainment really knocks you back. There are hours and hours of licensed music here, all carefully handpicked to add to the 80s ambience. The music is peppered with humorous banter from a host of DJs. You'll find tons of bands and artists, including Quiet Riot, Michael Jackson, David Lee Roth, Herbie Hancock, Judas Priest, and Frankie Goes to Hollywood. There are hours and hours of music in the game, and once you get tired of one genre, flipping to the next is as easy as changing the station. When you stop the car and just listen to the radio as the cars cross the street and jets arc across the sky, with some Haitians having a shootout with the Cubans across the street, it's then that you realise that Rockstar had one hell of a lot of fun constructing this game.
◼️ [b]Voice acting[/b]
I once had a dream: Machete said to me that I had big cojones. It wasn’t a dream. [b]Danny Trejo, Butch Cassidy, Dennis Hopper, Philip Michael Thomas[/b], those are only some of the most famous actors that played a huge role in the voice acting of this masterpiece. 

[h2][b]Extra[/b][/h2]
◼️ [b]Replayability[/b] 
Mostly for nostalgia, like I did after listening to a Phil Collins greatest hits (I was mistaken, he was in GTA Vice City Stories, another great Rockstar Game forgotten in their archives) 
◼️ [b]Game length[/b]
Around 20 hours, with a lot of trial and error on some missions.

[h1]
WHAT ISN'T WORKING OUT?
[/h1]
◼️ Graphically speaking it aged pretty bad. I patched the client with the PS2 patch, it’s a small improvement on performance and gameplay (more pedestrian and cars on screen and higher field of vision)
◼️ The plot is kind of short and some quests and plotlines end without a real developing between Tommy and the characters.
◼️ The mouse and keyboard binds are great for cars and bikes but not for flying. Some missions with planes and helicopters are a real nightmare.

Some minor, nothing game-breaking.

Vice City is probably the best GTA that has been made to date. Obviously, as a PC gamer, this opinion does not include GTA V as that one was never released by Rockstar on my favourite platform. I personally liked GTA IV a lot and the reviews on the latest installment were very promising - I just think Vice City was more captivating than the rest.

Vice City looks dated, yes. Please bear in mind that this is an eleven year old game and considering the capacity of our smart phones this game is accessible as an Android application as the game's engine can easily be handled by our phones' hardware. Its atmosphere, however, is still captivating even a decade after its release so playing such an "old" game on a widescreen monitor with next-gen hardware is no shame!

You play as Tommy Vercetti (voice by Ray Liotta) and you are in the '80s. You have cars, music and even film references from this era. Some scenes remind you of Miami Vice while others are clearly a nod to Pacino's character in Scarface. How cool is that?

You have dozens of missions available. Some continue the main story while other are just side missions. Each includes a cutscene with amazing voice acting so it is a crime to skip any of the available missions. Oh, you don't want to do any of these? No problem: Vice City allows the player to just cruise in the city, steal cars, crash these cars, harass citizens (with these cars, too). You can drive a cab and earn some money at your leisure. Or steal a police car and become the terminator of vigilantes.

There are tons of things to do in GTA. And while Vice City is certainly an outdated game nothing else out there can remind you how cool the '80s were than this piece of treasure.

So you might be asking why review a game that originally came out in 2002/2003? Well to this day it is still my favorite game. Nothing has come close to beating it and i don’t think anything ever will. 

There’s been a lot of controversy over the years about the Grand Theft Auto games, and their potential effects on children; so, this is probably a bad time to mention that I first played Vice City when I was quite young. 
But onto why I love the game so much: it’s probably a mixture of nostalgia and obsession. I believe that it would be in my top 5 games that I’ve spent the most time on (I’ve probably beaten it 12 times), and it’s quite ultimately the game I am the most familiar with.

One of the more-objectively strong reasons why I love Vice City over the other GTA games is that Tommy Vercetti, as a main character, makes the most sense. It’s out of character for the majority of GTA characters to run around on a rampage. Vercetti is a sandpaper-rough, heartless shell of a man: he only wants to get the money back that was stolen from him, and he’ll work with whoever he can to achieve his goals. Some people may see him as a bit of a shallow character, but I’d rather that over a bad-guy-turned-good, like a lot of the other main characters in the GTA series. It just makes no sense for Niko (from GTA IV) to mow down dozens of pedestrians, when a lot of his dialogue is about the horrors of war back in his homeland, and how he is coming to the US to make himself a new life. Plus he first appears wearing a light blue-green Hawaiian shirt i mean what is there not to love.

Much like the cast of characters, the story of Vice City worked so wonderfully because the developers threw it all against the backdrop of the nineteen eighties, which was in itself just a rip roaring time to be alive. At least that’s the impression one gets from games and television. You know, if you ignored the cold war, economic recession and the bad hairstyles. Vice City won in my eyes as it was a straight up gangster story. It certainly helped that it was basically a retelling of Scarface. If you’re going to make an 80s gangster movie there’s no better source material.

Now onto the most-subjective reason why I love the game, even more so than pure nostalgia: the radio stations, or more specifically: V Rock. I still have the entire audio file of the station on my computer, and I’d listen to it separate from the game. I listen to it while i’m driving around today so that must count for something. 

V Rock is still for me the pinnacle of in game music. As someone who wasn’t that into music in my younger days, I can thank V Rock for introducing me to the bands I would still be listening to today. 2 Minutes to Midnight by Iron Maiden, Bark at the Moon from Ozzy, Cum On Feel The Noize by Quiet Riot, Twisted Sister, Motley Crue and many more. Classic metal at its finest. It was also hosted by everyone’s favourite radio host Lazlow, of Chatterbox fame.

This isn’t to say that Vice City is a perfect game, but then again I personally believe that a critical part of loving something is realising that it’s not perfect, and being okay with its faults. The game has some pretty obtrusive shooting controls, because of the early lock-on mechanic. It’s the same sort of issue that the other PS2-era GTAs had. This makes the shooting parts of gameplay quite unnecessarily hard. Not that I dislike a hard game, but I want to at least feel as though I am in control when I am getting the crap shot out of my character. 

To summarise, Vice City is a great combination of atmosphere, story, characters, and soundtrack. If you’re only familiar with the Grand Theft Auto games with fancy graphics on current-gen consoles, then you really should give Vice City a try. 

You can thank me later!

This PS2 classic expands and improves upon GTA III in every possible way. More than just an incremental update, Vice City feels like a true leap forward, perfectly capturing the look, sound, and spirit of 1980s American pop culture. From its neon soaked streets to its over the top fashion and cars, every detail radiates that decade’s excess and flair. The soundtrack is legendary packed with iconic pop, rock, and new wave tracks, it remains one of the greatest licensed playlists ever compiled for a video game. Cruising through the city at night while blasting these hits is still one of gaming’s most memorable experiences. Narratively, Vice City wears its influences on its sleeve. It borrows heavily from Scarface and Miami Vice, crafting a story of crime, ambition, and betrayal that feels cinematic without ever losing its tongue in cheek charm. The late Ray Liotta brings real star power as Tommy Vercetti, delivering a performance that pays homage to his Goodfellas persona while adding a unique edge that makes the character unforgettable. Gameplay wise, the improvements over GTA III are there but not vastly improved. Players now have motorcycles, helicopters, and an expanded arsenal of weapons, not to mention a more vibrant and varied open world to explore. The ability to purchase properties and businesses added a sense of progression and ownership that deepened the experience beyond simple missions. Overall, Vice City is worth playing and the OG version more so since the remaster does not have the licencing to bring back all the songs they have here.

[h1]The time to take over the city is now.[/h1]

[b][i]Grand Theft Auto: Vice City[/i][/b] is an open-world action game released in 2002. Fresh out of prison, and sent to the eponymous city for a drug deal that swiftly goes wrong, Tommy Vercetti must carve his name in the criminal underworld, gather back the assets he lost, and hopefully raise his own empire.

[h3]Show me your bright lights, and your city lights![/h3]

Welcome to the wonderful world of 80’s Florida, with its vivid neon-soaked nights and beautiful tropical sunrises. The tonal shift from [i]Grand Theft Auto III[/i] is such that, even in the gloomiest and darkest of storms, Vice City is pleasantly saturated and bathed in light. Even character animation has been bumped up a notch, as they feature more natural movement. Of course, such an old title suffers on the technical side, with fairly primitive pedestrian and scenery models, as well as basic textures and limited draw distance. Occasional seams in the world geometry show up in the poorer parts of the mainland, while the cutscene character models have uncanny facial animation. 

No crashes or performance issues on my Ryzen 9 3900X, 64GB RAM, 1070 Ti, Windows 10 system. However, this title has barebones modern system support – widescreen resolutions tend to stretch UI elements, some visual elements like flares can flicker, crosshairs are not aligned with where your weapons actually hit, and there are a host of minor physics bugs that aggravate to game-breaking levels when the “Frame Limiter” is disabled. Highly advise installing basic community fixes for improved resolution detection and a decent play experience.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2612980855
[h3]Tuuuurn up, the raaaadio…[/h3]

Words struggle to express how awesome the soundtrack in this title is – or indeed, the entirety of the radio. Enjoy the absolute biggest hits of the 80s from the likes of Laura Branigan, Ozzy Osbourne, The Buggles, and countless more. From power ballads to new-wave, the music is absolutely splendid. In case this doesn’t cement its quality, the first song you’ll hear when you enter a vehicle is the sensational “Billie Jean” by Michael Jackson. The radio even includes hilarious talk shows and commercials, poking fun at the 80s’ trends and society. Seriously, my only gripe with the radio is that not every vehicle can enjoy it. Emergency services have occasional dispatcher and patrol dialogue, which are still comical, but I wanna hear Gary Numan’s “Cars” again!

Phew. Moving on through the sound category, voice acting has received some welcome improvements too, beyond a mere bitrate bump. Big names such as Ray Liotta and Burt Reynolds are among the cast, providing high quality dialogue in and outside of cutscenes. Meanwhile, sound effects are of a good variety, while weapons are notably punchy and satisfying. 

[h3]Okay guys. Nice and easy, just as we planned.[/h3]

The primary gameplay loop has been largely unchanged from [i]Grand Theft Auto III[/i], with only minor tweaks for convenience. The player controls Tommy throughout the city, on-foot and in various vehicles. Driving is much better across the board in this installment, and you have some degree of in-air and post-rollover control, thus letting you salvage botched jumps or stunts. Motorcycles are also introduced, boasting extraordinary nimbleness on the ground, while aircraft such as helicopters are ideal for rapid transportation across the city. Do be mindful of where you park your stuff – your rides tend to disappear if you wander too far away from them outside of garages, which is annoying.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2612982162

Outside of cars, Tommy has access to an even wider array of weapons. Each equipment slot can contain one of at least two weapons for it, so there’s a small tactical choice to be made in certain cases. The reality, however, is that the gunplay is still pretty poor. Even with keyboard-and-mouse controls offering pinpoint precision, attacking with anything has an unpleasant delay as your character must raise the weapon and shoot, usually compounded by zero mobility while firing. One would be wise to take advantage of jumping and crouching to cancel some animation and get back into the fight faster.

Dirty tricks or not, these may be required in the more hectic parts of the game. Tommy is highly vulnerable to gunfire, especially when rooted by said unwieldy weapons and standing close to enemies who suddenly switch to burst-fire. He also suffers from some aggravating syndromes: the sprinting endurance of someone with no lungs, and a tendency to dissolve in water higher than waist-deep. The latter is especially tragic, when the game world is surrounded by water. Yet another stupid death.

[h3]I think this could be the beginning of a beautiful business relationship.[/h3]

When intrepid players are not engaging in wanton chaos and destruction, they might fancy partaking in missions. The objectives are usually straightforward: drive here or there, shoot here or there, and sometimes escape pursuers. While many missions have memorable moments in and of themselves via unique interactions or scripting, the real winner is the approach flexibility. Why drive across the city and struggle to avoid roadblocks and firing squads in a rickety sedan, when you can airlift to safety?

All good to know when difficulty is seemingly all over the place, depending on the order you tackle missions in. You may finish a mission after killing the lone target, but on the next you get the police throwing everything they’ve got on you and your extremely frail and stupid escort target – or the other way around! And on that note, the escorted are a pain in the backside, falling behind and getting stuck in the level; not to mention the police, who spawn incessantly whenever you attain more than two wanted stars.

[h3]I run this town now. ME![/h3]

Most missions reward the player with some amount of money. Fairly generous, until you realize that there are several devious money gates in the game’s third act, and that, by completing only the necessary missions, your funds may be on the limited side. The player is supposed to purchase property – which is only explained twice in easy-to-miss contexts - and do various errands for said assets before it counts towards unlocking the last story arc. Some properties have really tedious requirements, so new players ought to reconsider buying the ice cream factory or strip club.

Losing all of your weapons on death or arrest is terribly costly, doubly so when your last save was several missions ago. On the other hand, side-missions in emergency or service vehicles provide exponential monetary rewards if done for long enough in one go, on top of other less-obvious diversions and challenges. Those who can exploit the side content will find money no issue.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2612984022
[h3]You take my self, you take my self control…[/h3]

Finishing the story could take some eight to ten hours. Existing side content roughly doubles that play-time. 100% completion – which also provides fun bonuses – can easily eat 20+ hours. There’s also a veritable collection of cheat codes to indulge in, should one fancy an afternoon of even greater silliness. While a full playthrough is fairly long lasting, replayability in itself is limited due to the overall linear nature of the story.

[h3]‘Cause when the feeling’s right,
I’m gonna run all night,
I’m gonna run to you![/h3]

Why would I review a game that came out 16 years ago?
Well, to see how this game holds up after all this time. How does it feel playing it with our modern age pc's and view of games in general. 
Short answer: It's still worth playing.
It has aging problems but the gameplay and story are still great and you should give it a try.
If you are a returning player, try completing it 100%. I surely had a blast doing it.
Below I go indepth looking at each fundamental part that makes Vice City.

[u]Story[/u]:
This is one of the selling points of GTA: Vice City! Rockstar delivers a well written scenario with a well paced character development. It's 1986. You play as Tommy Vercetti (who we first saw in GTA III), a Liberty City based mobgang member  who just got out of jail. Sonny, the mafiaboss decides it's in everyone's interest if Tommy doesn't gets interfered with the mafia's bussiness for a while since a lot of people will recognise him in the moody Libery City streets so he sends Tommy off to the beautiful, warm and sunny southern city of Vice City (read Miami) to overlook an exchange between the mafia and some other gang. The exchange gets messed up and Tommy loses the drugs AND the money. So Tommy is stuck in Vice City to get Sonny his money back but also build a new reputation for himself. This is the setup. Vice City is the city of opportunity and you will have to make friends, steal a lot of money and kill your way up the influence ladder.
What makes the story more immersive than GTA III is the much improved cutscenes. They now have actual well written dialogue. The people you meet all have more defined characteristics. Ofcourse this is a game from 2002/2003 so the models don't have distinct fascial expression but they did a really good job with making them feel alive and with a soul.

[u]Gameplay[/u]:
You will complete missions to advance in the story. These missions, along with some side-activities, are the main gameplay elements in Vice City. There is a good variety. All the classics are here: follow someone without being detected, kill person A and B, steal money from person C, rob a bank, get notorious and eventually own the city.
Gunplay: improved from GTA III. Aiming is still a bit wonky. Only AR's can use iron sights. Enemy hitboxes make sense and shooting somebody's head off is very satisfying!
Also a small detail: you can't swim... People just couldn't swim in 1986.

[u]Graphics[/u]:
When reviewing older games you cannot compare the graphics with today's standards. So let's look at the year it got released: 2002. What games can we compare Vice City with? Hitman 2, Warcraft: Reign of chaos, Elder scrolls: Morrowind, Jedi Knight 2,... People were really amazed by the graphical improvement VC brought and I will join those people. Replaying this, I didn't mind the older, simple graphics. The colours are bright and reflect the Miami atmosphere Rockstar tries to bring into the game.

[u]Sound[/u]:
The music in this game is top notch. A well selected range of popular and unpopular songs made in the 80's are scattered across 9 different radio stations. You will definitely sing along while driving around. It better be good since a huge portion of the game you will be inside a car, listening to the radio. The different genres are a bit less distinct as they were in GTA 3.
An important note: because of expired music licenses, some (iconic) songs have been removed from the Steam version but you can fix this by replacing the radio audio files with the ones from the original version. If you don't have it you can download the files from one of the guides in the community tab.
The sound effects used in Vice City are much improved if we compare them with its predecessor. No more wierd reverb and cut samples. Sounds sound clearer, you can make out easier where they are coming from and are overall just more realistic (considering it's 2002).

[u]Performance[/u]: 
It's bad... on modern systems. You will need unofficial, player created patches to run this game on an acceptable level. Look, if this was an old game from a small compagny I would have no problems with it but this is Rockstar's heritage. They do not seem to care to update their games to run on modern computers. GTA III has the same problem and even GTA IV runs so bad (it actually always did on pc but that's another story). A big thanks to the people who create the unofficial patches! It  fixes most crashes, fixes the fonts of ingame text and gives the hud a HD update + fixes a lot of bugs. Oh right, one last thing: Vice City runs at 30 fps. Yes there's an option to turn off the frame limiter but that makes the game unplayable since it makes the physics go crazy. There isn't a mod out there to fix this so get used to it. Also, I had some issues with my game freezing up for like 1 second once in a while. This too has something to do with running this on modern hardware.

[u]Physics[/u]:
When the game came out pretty much nobody bothered to care about the bad physics because the game was fresh, graphics were bright and new but today the game doesn't has those percs anymore. The physics will make you bash your keyboard more than once. Lightpoles are your biggest enemy in Vice City. You drive 180km/h and go to zero in about 0.1 second by hitting poles next to the road. It's crazy. They're like black holes. Also cars behave very strange. They will change speed instantly as if they were on rails that leads them around. NPC's will get stuck a lot which is very frustrating when playing missions were you have to save them from dying. Just do the ambulance mission if you want to know what I'm talking about. Also, when driving close to the sidewalk, pedestrians will jump away to try avoiding you hitting them. The funny thing is they very frequently jump IN FRONT of your car. This is pretty hilarious until the cops start doing this...
Stealing cars and driving around town is the core activity in all GTA games, hence the name, so it better be good. Luckily it is. They used the same engine from GTA III where they allready nailed down the driving physics. It's arcadey ofcourse but using your handbrake to drift in corners feels really good and can be done without any hassle.

[u]AI[/u]:
Another aspect that could be done better. The AI in Vice City is smarter than the AI in GTA III but it's still far from good. Some missions require you to complete them with an AI partner. They have to be driven around, they cannot die and you cannot leave them behind so you have to look after them. It gets very frustrating when that npc gets stuck walking into a wall or a random spawned car runs him/her over. This happens a lot and nothing you can do about it.
The AI controlling the cops is.. interesting. They will swarm you like dogs with rabis. They have zero strategy or intelligence. They throw themselfs on you with their cars and hope for the best. Even on foot they will get stuck when you walk behind a wall, not being able to find a way to go behind it. This may be in your advantage but it just feels messed up.
AI never seeks cover or fires you from a position where they have an advantage. They will just run up to you like the bombheads from Serious Sam.

[u]Map[/u]:
Maps are very important in open world games. A good map is filled with stuff to do, feels alive and has interesting geography. Does VC deliver? I would say yes.
The map is beautiful and colourful. There are many people and cars moving around town so the map feels alive too. There are many side activities and they are scattered around the map. If you complete the game you will be familier with the whole city.
Ofcourse you could say it's not that big but in 2002 this was a normal sized map.

I had a lot of fun completing this game 100% and reliving the Vice City feels. GTA: Vice City will always be one of the best GTA's Rockstar ever made. A true classic of the open world mayhem games.
I hope you enjoyed reading my review!
